entries.text: What the law does not say. It does not change the next toss. After any run of tails, a fair coin still has conditional probability \(1/2\) of heads on the following toss: the tosses are independent. The proportion moves toward \(1/2\) because later tosses dilute the early ones. Reading a deficit of heads as a debt the coin must repay is the gambler's fallacy. The weak law also speaks about probabilities at each \(n\), rather than about one infinite sequence being eventually trapped near \(\mu\). That pathwise statement is the strong law: if the \(X_i\) are independent and identically distributed with finite mean \(\mu\), then \(P(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar X_n=\mu)=1\).

Scope and error. The limit needs iid sampling and a finite positive variance only. Existence of a moment generating function is an extra assumption used by the proof below, not a hypothesis of the theorem. For a finite sample the limit is used as an approximation. The error depends on skewness. In the Edgeworth expansion the first correction beyond \(\Phi\) is proportional to the skewness \(\gamma=E[(X_1-\mu)^3]/\sigma^3\), divided by \(\sqrt{n}\). A symmetric summand has \(\gamma=0\), so that term drops out. The Berry–Esseen theorem bounds the largest gap between \(P(Z_n\le a)\) and \(\Phi(a)\) by a universal constant times \(E[|X_1-\mu|^3]/(\sigma^3\sqrt{n})\). An exponential summand has skewness \(2\), so its leading correction is of exact order \(1/\sqrt{n}\).

Joint moment generating function. For a pair \((X,Y)\), define \(M_{X,Y}(s,t)=E[e^{sX+tY}]\) wherever the expectation is finite. When this function is finite on an open neighbourhood of the origin, it determines the joint distribution. On such a neighbourhood, \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if and only if \(M_{X,Y}(s,t)=M_X(s)M_Y(t)\).
